passage:
Omkar,
I owe you an apology, a proper one, not a quick "sorry" in the corridor.
When the class trip money went missing from the monitor's desk, I told Ma'am I was sure it was you. You wouldn't look at anyone, you kept tapping your pen, and your voice went shaky. I thought that was proof.
Yesterday the money turned up in the sports-room register, where the monitor had left it. Nobody took it.
My cousin, who studies psychology, told me that nervous people telling the truth can look exactly like that, and people who lie can look perfectly calm. I didn't know that. You were probably nervous because I was staring at you.
I'm sorry I made the whole class look at you that way. I'll tell Ma'am too.
Kiran

qa.q: Where did the trip money turn up?
qa.a: In the sports-room register, where the monitor had left it.

qa.q: Why was Kiran so sure Omkar had taken the money?
qa.a: Kiran believed that not looking at anyone, tapping a pen and a shaky voice were proof of lying.

qa.q: What could Kiran do differently the next time something goes missing?
qa.a: Kiran could check the facts first, such as where the money was last kept, instead of reading guilt from nervousness.

qa.q: What was it like for Omkar to be suspected in front of the class?
qa.a: Omkar was probably frightened and humiliated, and being stared at likely made the nervousness even stronger.

grounding: A teenager who took fidgeting and avoided eye contact as proof of lying learns such cues are weak, since nervous truth-tellers look the same.

passage:
What did I learn in Class 11? That I'm terrible at spotting liars. I'm Baljeet, and so is everyone, probably.
During the student council election, someone ran an anonymous page mocking the candidates. Everyone suspected a quiet boy from 11C, because when the teacher questioned him he stammered, went red and stared at his shoes. I was sure too.
Then my friend Bidisha looked me straight in the eye and said, "It's horrible. I'd never do that." Totally calm. I believed her completely.
Two weeks later the school found the page had been made from her account.
So now when someone says "you can tell by their eyes", I think of that boy's red face and Bidisha's steady one. I check facts now, not faces.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say when asked about the page?
qa.a: "It's horrible. I'd never do that."

qa.q: Why did Baljeet believe Bidisha so completely?
qa.a: Bidisha looked Baljeet straight in the eye and stayed totally calm, which Baljeet took as a sign of honesty.

qa.q: What does Baljeet do now instead of reading faces?
qa.a: Baljeet checks facts, not faces, since both the steady eyes and the red cheeks turned out to be misleading.

qa.q: How might the quiet boy from 11C have felt while everyone suspected him?
qa.a: He likely felt scared and ashamed, which made him stammer and go red even though he had done nothing.

grounding: A teenager learns that a calm, eye-contact denial and a stammering, red-faced one say little about who is honest.

passage:
At the career fair in their Pune college, the man at the glossy stall had an easy laugh and the same football jersey Zubin wore on weekends. "Guaranteed paid internship," he said. "Just a small registration fee today." Zubin liked him instantly and reached for his wallet.
Payal from the placement office, who always mumbled and never met anyone's eyes, hovered nearby. "Um... none of the stalls charge fees," she said. Zubin almost laughed her off. She seemed so awkward.
Then he stopped. Why did he trust the jersey guy more? Because he was fun? He checked the college's official placement list on his phone. No such company. When he looked up, the stall was already packing. He found Payal. "Thank you. I nearly didn't listen."

qa.q: What did the man at the stall ask Zubin to pay?
qa.a: A small registration fee today.

qa.q: Why did Zubin almost laugh Payal off?
qa.a: She seemed awkward, mumbling and avoiding eye contact, so Zubin doubted her while trusting the friendly man in the familiar jersey.

qa.q: What protective step helped Zubin?
qa.a: He paused, asked himself why he trusted the charming man, and checked the college's official placement list before paying.

qa.q: How might Payal feel when Zubin thanks her?
qa.a: She would probably feel noticed and valued, after nearly being dismissed for seeming awkward.

grounding: A young man notices he trusts a charming, familiar-seeming stranger and doubts an awkward staff member, and checks the facts before paying.

"The first guy was great," Pradeep said, dropping onto the sofa. "Same college as me, loves cricket, so easy to talk to."
"And the second?" Bhavna asked.
"Bit awkward. Didn't laugh at my jokes. Kept checking his notes."
"Did the first one give references?"
"He said he'd send them later. Why?"
"Because the second one brought his last landlord's number, a salary slip and his ID. The first one wants us to skip the agreement because 'we're all friends here'."
Pradeep paused. "Huh. I just... liked him."
"That's the point. Liking someone isn't the same as being able to trust them. People who want to trick you often make themselves very easy to like."

qa.q: What step do they agree on, and why is it wise?
qa.a: They agree to call both references tomorrow, checking facts instead of relying on who seemed likeable.

qa.q: How might the second applicant be judged unfairly without Bhavna's point?
qa.a: He might be turned down just for seeming awkward, even though he was the one who brought real proof.

passage:
In Lisbon, Pablo had found the perfect flat: bright, near the metro, suspiciously cheap. The owner wrote beautifully. He was working abroad, he explained, and would post the keys once the deposit arrived. He even sent a photo of a passport.
"He sounds so genuine," said Pablo's flatmate Bilal. "Honestly, I trust him."
"I trust him too," Pablo said. "That's why I'm checking." He didn't judge the man's warmth; he checked what could be checked. The property register listed a different owner. The same kitchen photos appeared on a listing in another city. And the owner wouldn't agree to a video viewing.
Pablo reported the advert to the website and sent nothing. Bilal read the results over his shoulder. "He told it so smoothly," he said quietly.

qa.q: What did the property register show?
qa.a: The property register listed a different owner.

qa.q: What does Pablo mean by "I trust him too. That's why I'm checking"?
qa.a: Pablo knows that a feeling of trust proves nothing, so he wants facts to back it up before sending money.

qa.q: Which checks protected Pablo, and why were they better than a gut feeling?
qa.a: He checked the property register, the photos and whether a video viewing was possible; records and independent sources can't be charmed.

qa.q: How does Bilal's view of the owner change?
qa.a: Bilal moves from full trust to quiet surprise, realising a smooth, confident story was not a sign of truth.

grounding: An adult checks a flat owner's claims through records, photos and a viewing request instead of trusting how sincere the messages feel.

passage:
In the foundation's small office, Kunal and Vandana had two grant applications left. The first founder had pitched beautifully: tears at the right moment, a story about teaching three hundred girls. The second had stammered through her slides and apologised twice.
"The first one, surely," Vandana said. "She was so sincere."
"Maybe," Kunal said. "Let's check." He phoned the village school the first founder had named; the headmaster had never heard of her programme. The attendance sheets she sent had the same handwriting on every page. The second applicant's numbers matched the block office records, and a local teacher confirmed her classes by phone.
Vandana sat back. "I was ready to give it to the better storyteller."
"Practice makes a story smooth," Kunal said. "Only checking tells you it's true."

qa.a: He phoned the named school, looked closely at the attendance sheets, and matched the second applicant's numbers with block office records, relying on evidence rather than impressions.

qa.q: What would have happened to the second applicant if only the pitches had counted?
qa.a: She would likely have lost the grant despite real work, just for stammering and seeming less confident.

grounding: An adult verifies two grant claims through a phone call, documents and official records, finding that the most fluent story was the false one.

passage:
In their small town, Uma trusted most people. When the new vegetable seller, Rehana, got the change wrong one morning, a neighbour whispered, "New here. Watch her." Uma just counted again with her. "Easy mistake," she said, and Rehana laughed and handed back the extra ten rupees.
That afternoon a man in a neat shirt knocked, saying he was from the electricity office and a fine had to be paid in cash today or the line would be cut.
Uma's heart jumped. Then she slowed down. "Please wait outside. I'll call the office." She rang the number printed on her last bill. The clerk said nobody had been sent and no fine was due. When she went back to the door, the man had gone. She reported it to the office and warned her neighbours that evening.

qa.q: What number did Uma ring?
qa.a: The number printed on her last bill.

qa.q: What did Uma feel when the man mentioned the fine, and how did she respond?
qa.a: Her heart jumped with fear, but she slowed down and chose to check rather than pay.

qa.q: Why did Uma treat the vegetable seller and the man at the door differently?
qa.a: A small mistake with change needed only ordinary trust, while a cash demand under threat was high-stakes, so she raised the bar and checked with the office.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel about Uma after the mix-up with the change?
qa.a: Rehana would likely feel respected and welcome, since Uma didn't join the whispering and treated it as an easy mistake.

grounding: A woman keeps ordinary trust with a new seller but raises the standard of proof for a threatening cash demand, avoiding both naivety and accusation.

passage:
In Class 9 I decided I needed to be on the quiz team, and Lokesh Sir picked the team. So I started telling him things. "Sir, your explanations are so much better than last year's." "Sir, that tie really suits you." "Sir, everyone says you're the best." I stayed behind to carry his books.
I wasn't actually thinking about his teaching. I was thinking about the list on the notice board.
One day he said, kindly, "Ayesha, thank you. The selection is a written test, though." My face went hot. He had seen through it, and he wasn't even angry.
Looking back, what embarrasses me isn't that I wanted the team. It's that I never once looked at him as a person, only as a door I wanted open.

qa.q: How did Lokesh Sir say the team would be selected?
qa.a: He said the selection is a written test.

qa.q: What was Ayesha really thinking about while praising Lokesh Sir?
qa.a: Ayesha was thinking about the list on the notice board, not about his teaching or about him as a person.

qa.q: What could Ayesha have done instead to try for the quiz team?
qa.a: Ayesha could have prepared for the written test and asked Lokesh Sir honestly how to get ready.

qa.q: How might Lokesh Sir have seen Ayesha's compliments?
qa.a: He seemed to see they were aimed at the selection, but he responded kindly rather than angrily.

grounding: A teenager looks back on showering a teacher with compliments to win a team place, praise aimed at an outcome rather than the person.

passage:
Coach's note, Under-16 football, 12 October.
For three weeks Asif has been following our captain, a Class 12 student, everywhere. He carries the captain's kit bag, laughs at every joke, and tells anyone nearby that the captain is "the best player this school has ever had". The captain told me, a little uncomfortably, that Asif keeps asking if he'll "put in a word" for the starting eleven.
Asif's own training has dropped off. He skipped two fitness sessions to watch senior practice instead.
Today I spoke to him privately. I said I've noticed the compliments, and that selection depends on what I see on the pitch, not on who the captain likes. He looked embarrassed. We agreed he will do extra passing drills on Tuesdays, and I'll give him honest feedback every Friday.
Nirmala Joseph

qa.q: How many fitness sessions did Asif skip?
qa.a: He skipped two fitness sessions to watch senior practice.

qa.q: What did Asif want from praising the captain?
qa.a: He wanted the captain to put in a word so he would get into the starting eleven.

qa.q: What did the coach do that could redirect Asif?
qa.a: The coach spoke to him privately, explained that selection depends on the pitch, and set extra passing drills with honest Friday feedback.

qa.q: How does the captain feel about Asif's praise?
qa.a: The captain seems uncomfortable, sensing the compliments are tied to a favour rather than real admiration.

grounding: A coach notices a teenage boy flattering an older student to win a team place, praise aimed at the outcome rather than the person.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Rafiq (Class 10) came in confused about friends. A group of seniors has been praising everything he does: his hair, his bike, his "genius" ideas. He loves it. His old friend Jagdish, meanwhile, told him plainly that skipping tuition to hang out with them was a bad idea, and also called his science project "brilliant, honestly".
Rafiq said, "Jagdish criticises me, so maybe he's jealous?" I asked him to notice who had ever disagreed with him, and who had ever asked him for something. He went quiet. The seniors had asked twice to borrow his bike and once for him to cover for them with a teacher.
By the end he said, "Jagdish says good things and bad things. The others only say good things when they want something." We will meet again next week.

qa.q: What had the seniors asked Rafiq for?
qa.a: They had asked twice to borrow his bike and once for him to cover for them with a teacher.

qa.q: What did Rafiq first think about Jagdish's criticism?
qa.a: He thought Jagdish might be jealous, because the criticism felt less pleasant than the seniors' praise.

qa.q: Which question from the counsellor helped Rafiq see clearly?
qa.a: Who had ever disagreed with him and who had ever asked him for something, which showed that the seniors' praise came with requests.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel if Rafiq keeps choosing the seniors?
qa.a: Jagdish might feel hurt and pushed aside, since his honesty came from care, praising and warning Rafiq without wanting anything.

grounding: A teenage boy learns that a friend who both praises and disagrees is more trustworthy than a group whose praise comes with requests.

Hafsa from final year sat with me at lunch again. She said I'm "so much more mature than the other first-years", that I have "leader energy", that she could tell the first time she saw me. I felt ten feet tall.
Then she told me about the "opportunity": sell some products, bring in two friends, pay a joining fee, "and you'll earn more than your parents". She said, "Someone like you won't overthink it."

Friday, 10 pm
Third time this month. Gopika stopped at my desk at 4:45 and said, "Nandini, your slides are always so elegant, I don't know how you do it." Two minutes later: "Could you take over the vendor report? Just this once?"
On Monday it was "you're the only one here who really gets spreadsheets" before asking me to fix her sheet. Last week, "you're such a good listener", then could I cover her Saturday.
Tonight I scrolled back through my messages. Every compliment from her came within ten minutes of a favour. When my manager praises me, she names something specific, like the chart on page six, and she does it when she wants nothing.
Maybe Gopika is overloaded and doesn't know how to ask. Maybe it's habit. Either way, next time I'll thank her for the kind words and decide about the favour separately.

First year in the hostel, I was so lonely I could hear my own heartbeat at night. Then I met Rehana in the mess queue. By day three I'd bought her earrings. By day five I was messaging her forty times a day and calling her my soul sister. I planned a holiday trip for us without asking her.
She started taking longer to reply. When she went to dinner with her roommates, I sent a long message about how hurt I was. She said, very gently, "Manjula, this is a lot, really fast."
I was furious at first. Now I see it. I wasn't building a friendship; I was trying to lock one in before it could leave. The counsellor I saw that term said the speed was the warning sign. We're friends now, slowly. Properly.

qa.a: Manjula had bought her earrings.

qa.q: What turning point helped Manjula change?
qa.a: Rehana's gentle "this is a lot, really fast" and seeing a counsellor helped Manjula recognise the speed as the warning sign and slow down.

qa.a: She probably felt overwhelmed and pressured, which is why she took longer to reply and named it gently.

qa.q: What did Ganga tell Tanya that was a wise step?
qa.a: Ganga said Tanya didn't have to decide anything quickly and could talk to the college counsellor or Ganga any time.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel if Tanya asks for more space?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and afraid of being left alone, given his loneliness, which could show up as more sulking.

grounding: An old schoolmate watches a young man flood a new partner with attention and big promises within days, and sees the intensity itself as the warning sign.
